beats.beat: The company reports two segments: creating infrastructure, and operating a ready-mix concrete plant.

Inside the infrastructure segment, the work is described in three buckets: railways (designing and constructing platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and laying of railway tracks), bridges (beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss bridges) and roadways (bituminous and concrete roads connecting highways and district roads).

The ready-mix concrete plant is a manufacturing facility at Kashimira, in Thane district, Maharashtra, which the company describes as a state-of-the-art facility with its own quality control systems. Ready-mix concrete is the same material the road and bridge contracts consume, so the plant sits inside the supply chain rather than beside it.

Contracts are won by tender, and the filing sets out the chain in six steps: the client floats a tender for a specific work, a pre-bid meeting resolves queries, the contractor bids if it meets the eligibility criteria, the job is awarded to the lowest quote by letter of acceptance, the contractor deposits a performance guarantee, and only then is the drawing issued and the site handed over.

That chain is the single most important fact about how this company earns money: award goes to the lowest bidder. Price is set by competition before a rupee of work is done, and the contract is only signed after the company has committed a performance guarantee.

The customer list is a roll-call of public bodies — Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation Ltd, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority and Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Ltd — alongside private names: Sky Way Infrastructure Private Limited, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel Private Ltd and Krypton Corp.

Then the concentration. Western Railway has been a client since 2006 and accounts for 52% of the orders on hand; customers at the top of the list accounted for 57% of total revenue in the year ended March 31, 2018.
Geographically the company describes itself as a major player in Mumbai that is consolidating across Maharashtra, and its only disclosed fixed facility is the Thane plant.

The filing's own list of strengths — box pushing technique in project execution, a management team with more than 20 years in infrastructure, a 'healthy order book' — are claims by the company, stated without the underlying order-book value in the material available here.

business.heading: What the company actually does
business.purpose: Explain the two segments, the work it executes, how contracts are won, who the customers are and how concentrated that customer base is.

beats.beat: Revenue from operations, converted from the filing's lakhs to ₹ crore. FY2014: ₹86.61 crore. FY2015: ₹90.21 crore. FY2016: ₹74.53 crore. FY2017: ₹73.44 crore. FY2018: ₹60.53 crore.
Profit before interest, depreciation and tax — the filing's EBITDA line. FY2014: ₹7.84 crore. FY2015: ₹9.46 crore. FY2016: ₹7.83 crore. FY2017: ₹6.76 crore. FY2018: ₹9.29 crore.
Net profit after adjustments, in ₹ crore. FY2014: ₹0.96 crore. FY2015: ₹0.78 crore. FY2016: ₹0.33 crore. FY2017: ₹0.16 crore. FY2018: ₹3.15 crore.

Read together, those three series tell a story that a single year's numbers would hide. Revenue fell roughly a third from the FY2015 peak to FY2018, yet EBITDA in FY2018 was within ₹0.17 crore of its five-year high, and profit after tax went from ₹15.86 lakhs in FY2017 to ₹314.66 lakhs in FY2018. On the disclosed figures, EBITDA margin in FY2018 works out to roughly 15% of revenue against roughly 10% in FY2015 — the company did more with less revenue in FY2018.
Total assets, as restated, stood at ₹82.32 crore at FY2018 end, against ₹70.62 crore at FY2014 end.

Borrowings split is the heart of the balance sheet. At FY2018, short-term borrowings were ₹35.37 crore and long-term borrowings ₹1.33 crore — roughly ₹36.70 crore of debt against ₹60.53 crore of revenue.

The trend inside those borrowings is the point. Short-term borrowings rose every year, from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014 to ₹35.37 crore in FY2018. Long-term borrowings went the other way, from ₹6.73 crore in FY2015 down to ₹1.33 crore in FY2018. The business is funded by working capital lines, not term debt.

On top of that, the company had availed ₹405.02 lakhs — about ₹4.05 crore — as unsecured loans as on March 31, 2018, repayable on demand. A demand for repayment is a call on cash the company does not control the timing of.

The filing states plainly that the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and that sustained negative cash flow could adversely affect the business, financial condition and results of operations. The amount and the specific years are not disclosed in the material available here.

Related to that, the filing flags failure to recover amounts from sundry debtors and trade receivables on time as a risk to its financial condition — the mirror image of a business that bills government departments.

beats.beat: Amit Bholanath Mishra is the promoter and managing director. He holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue issued, subscribed and paid-up equity capital.

The rest of the register is thin. Hatim Sakerwala, a key management person, holds 9% of the equity, and three whole-time directors — Bharat kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — hold 300 shares each. Pre-issue, the company effectively has two meaningful holders.

The key management team is young and recently credentialed: Ms. Anchal Pachori, 28, is chief financial officer and a chartered accountant, and Mr. Mohit Soni, 26, is company secretary and compliance officer and an associate member of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India.

On the standard checks, the filing is clean. None of the directors is on the RBI list of willful defaulters, no criminal cases or investigations are recorded against any director, and the promoter has confirmed he has not been declared a willful defaulter by the RBI or any other government authority.

Related-party dealings are disclosed with figures. In FY2018 the company took loans of ₹68.4 lakhs from key management personnel or the board of directors, paid ₹57.7 lakhs in director remuneration, and carried ₹324.3 lakhs of outstanding payables to related parties as on 31.03.2018. The filing also flags that it has entered into related-party transactions in the past and may continue to do so.

A harder flag sits at page 18: two companies promoted by the promoter, Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited, were struck off by the Registrar of Companies on March 12, 2016 and March 11, 2016 respectively due to non-operation of business.

And a live one: the company, its promoter and its directors are currently involved in litigation pending at various stages, and the filing warns that an adverse decision could render them liable to liabilities and penalties. The nature and the amount at stake are not set out in the material available here.

One further disclosure worth connecting to the objects of the issue: the company has issued equity shares in the last 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price. Any incoming investor is buying at a level the company's recent issuances may not support.

beats.beat: The sector is defined broadly in the filing: infrastructure and construction covers power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure development.

Structure matters more than size for a company this small. The filing calls it a highly fragmented and working-capital-intensive market that contributes roughly 8% of India's GDP at constant prices. Fragmented means no one sets the price; working-capital-intensive means every contract consumes cash before it produces it.
The headline demand number the filing cites: India needs investment worth ₹50 trillion (US$777.73 billion) in infrastructure by 2022 for sustainable development.

Other sizing in the filing's industry chapter: foreign direct investment in construction development, townships and built-up infrastructure from April 2000 to December 2017 stood at US$24.67 billion, and the logistics sector was expected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 10.5% from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020. The chapter also carries construction-market estimates of US$400 billion in 2015 rising to US$1,000 billion by 2025, which the extraction flags as low confidence — present them as the filing's cited third-party estimates, not as the company's own numbers.

The demand drivers named are policy-led: the 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All; eased FDI norms across 15 sectors including real estate and construction; and the slow-moving backdrop of industrialisation, urbanisation, rising disposable income and population growth. Infrastructure spending was 9.0% of GDP in the 12th Five-Year Plan.

The headwinds are the filing's own, listed in its SWOT: the slow pace of government projects, a working-capital crunch that may affect profitability, and changes in government policy. For a company whose customers are government bodies and whose single largest client is a railway zone, these are not hypothetical.
On competition the filing is candid but unspecific: the company operates in a competitive industry with competitors in both the organised and the unorganised sector. No competitor is named.

The regulatory frame the business sits inside is set out across the filing's statutes chapter: the Companies Act, 2013, goods and services tax on supply of goods and services, the Factories Act, 1948 for labour in factories, and environmental law including the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild Limited is a Mumbai infrastructure contractor. It builds railways, bridges and roads, mostly for government bodies, and it runs a ready-mix concrete plant in Thane district, Maharashtra. Those are its two reported business segments.
What is being sold is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each. The issue price is printed as ₹[•] — not disclosed in the filing excerpt.
The objects section names one use: ₹1,130 lakhs for working capital requirements, plus a general corporate purposes line whose amount is redacted.

The tension a reader should hold in mind: revenue fell every year from FY2015 to FY2018, from ₹90.21 crore to ₹60.53 crore, while profit after tax jumped to ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 from ₹0.16 crore in FY2017.
The company is asking the public for money to fund the working capital that its own business model consumes — it already carries ₹35.37 crore of short-term borrowings against ₹60.53 crore of revenue.

intro.purpose: Orient a newcomer: what A B Infrabuild does, what it is selling, what the money is for, and the single tension — shrinking revenue against a sharp profit jump.

beats.beat: The issue is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 face value each, offered at a price the DRHP prints as ₹[•]. The price, the price band and the multiple of face value are not disclosed in the material available.

A primary offer can raise money in two ways: new shares issued by the company (a fresh issue, where the cash goes to the business) and existing shares sold by current holders (an offer for sale, where the cash goes to those sellers). The filing excerpt presents a single line of 44,28,000 shares and does not split the two, and no selling shareholder is named.

Of the objects named, one is quantified: ₹1,130 lakhs to meet working capital requirements. That is the bulk of what the reader can actually hold on to — the issue is funding the cash cycle that a lowest-bid contractor has to carry.
The second object, general corporate purposes, carries the amount as a redacted entry in the filing. General corporate purposes is a flexible bucket; how much lands in it is not disclosed.

Three disclosures sit against the objects and are worth the reader's attention: no independent agency has been appointed to appraise the proposed project, no monitoring agency has been appointed, and deployment of the funds is at the discretion of the management and the board, monitored by the audit committee.
The issue is run by Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited as lead manager, with Bigshare Services Private Limited as registrar to the issue.

beats.beat: These are drawn from the filing's own business-specific risk factors. Each is a claim about this company, not a general warning about IPOs.

Customer concentration. The filing states that the majority of revenues will depend on one customer, Indian Railways, its largest customer, contributing 57% of revenue in Fiscal 2018, and that losing Indian Railways would result in a significant dip in revenues. The order book tells the same story: Western Railway alone is 52% of orders on hand. One client, one award cycle, one budget.

The revenue model depends on winning bids, and won bids can be taken away. Revenues largely depend on acceptance of bids submitted to government and government departments — if the majority of bids are not awarded, performance suffers; and contracts in the order book may be adjusted, cancelled or suspended by clients, so the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenues or earnings.

Negative cash flow. The company had negative cash flow in recent financial years, and the filing warns that sustained negative cash flow could adversely impact the business, financial condition and results of operations. Alongside it the filing flags that failure to recover amounts from sundry debtors and trade receivables on time might affect financial condition.

Demand-repayable debt on top of rising short-term borrowings. ₹405.02 lakhs was outstanding as unsecured loans as on March 31, 2018, repayable on demand, and any demand from those lenders may affect cash flow and financial condition — sitting on a balance sheet where short-term borrowings have climbed from ₹30.82 crore in FY2014 to ₹35.37 crore in FY2018 against ₹60.53 crore of revenue.

Governance overhang from the promoter's earlier companies. Two companies promoted by the promoter were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation of business. Separately, the company, its promoter and its directors are involved in pending litigation, with an adverse outcome carrying liabilities and penalties. Neither the quantum nor the current stage of that litigation is disclosed in the material available here.

beats.beat: An Indian issue price is not set by the company alone: it is determined by the company in consultation with the lead manager, and justified in the filing against accounting ratios.

The company's face value is ₹10 per equity share. The issue price is ₹[•], and the filing states that the issue price is [•] times the face value. Both blanks are redacted, so the price at which any comparison would be struck is not disclosed.

The filing does carry the machinery for a peer comparison: a section headed 'Comparison of Accounting Ratios with Peer Group Companies' appears at page 55, and a basis-for-issue-price table at page 54. The extraction captures figures — 12.59 and 3.82 for FY2018 in one table, 4.14 for FY2016, 1.97 for FY2017 and 28.14 for FY2018 in another, and 12.39 and 44.71 in the peer comparison — but not the column headings that say which ratio each number is, and not the names of any peer company.

So the reader gets a comparison table without the two things that make it useful: peer names and metric labels. Named peers, their P/E, EPS, NAV and RoNW, are not in the material available, and the issue price is redacted. Peer multiples cannot be applied to an undisclosed price to produce a range.

What can be said is narrower and still worth saying: the FY2018 restated net profit was ₹314.66 lakhs and the promoter held 74,95,476 shares pre-issue, so the disclosed earnings are what they are — the filing's own arithmetic on the issue price is not available for a reader to check.
